newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD wants higher demand to boost jobs.
newsitem.headline: German SPD wants higher demand to boost jobs.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Tuesday called for a programme of measures to boost domestic spending as a way to alleviate record unemployment.

In a New Year news conference, party chairman Oskar Lafontaine attacked Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government for letting welfare costs rise and reducing the tax burden on industry while unemployment rose to post-war record levels.

"Ideas such as pay restraint, annual cuts in corporate taxation, annual cuts in social security benefits and a refusal to engage in international macroeconomic cooperation have achieved no improvement in the job market," Lafontaine said.
"You can't keep strangling domestic demand and then ask why investment isn't picking up."

Lafontaine called on the government urgently to ease the tax burden on workers and families to produce this stimulus in domestic demand, which analysts say has so far failed to materialise in an economic recovery driven mostly by exports.
Lafontaine pledged to oppose proposals by Kohl's coalition to raise value added tax (VAT) in order to be able to cut peak income tax rates.
The plan is part of a wide-ranging tax reform scheme, much of which will need approval from the SPD dominated upper house, the Bundesrat.

"The coalition can say goodbye to the idea right now, it has no chance of coming about. We said from the outset that we would not cooperate in raising VAT for social security recipients, pensioners, the unemployed and for middle income earners just so that a tax present can be made to high earners," he said.
Instead, Lafontaine repeated an SPD proposal to raise tax on energy consumption with the aim of reducing the level of social security contributions.
Lafontaine also accused the government of unsettling investors by constantly changing its taxation plans, and of fomenting social unrest with its programme of welfare cuts.
"Social peace is a factor in Germany's viability as an economic location," he said.
Lafontaine's ideas were immediately challenged by Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union, Kohl's coalition partners.

"It remains completely unclear how Lafontaine wants to structure and pay for lower taxes for workers and immediate cuts in social security contributions," Glos said. "Lafontaine makes absolutely no mention of the structural reform needed to ensure the survival of the social security system."

The SPD leader reiterated his support for a European single currency in 1999, but declined to say what he thought should happen if Germany or its major EU partners failed to meet the strict economic criteria to qualify for monetary union (EMU).
Lafontaine also said monetary union in itself was not enough, and must be accompanied by a coordinated EU-wide economic and financial policy aimed at job creation.
"EMU will only lead to more growth and employment if member states closely coordinate their economic and finance policies," he said.
